title: MIND Diet Linked to Slower Brain Aging in Long-Term Study
summary:
A diet that combines elements of the Mediterranean diet with an eating plan designed to lower blood pressure may help slow some of the structural changes that occur as the brain ages, according to research published online in the Journal of Neurology Neurosurgery & Psychiatry.

The plan is called the MIND diet, short for Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay. It emphasizes green leafy vegetables, other vegetables, berries, nuts, whole grains, fish, beans, olive oil and poultry. It recommends limiting butter and margarine, cheese, red meat, pastries and sweets, and fried fast foods.

Participants had regular health evaluations, and starting in 1999 they also received MRI brain scans. Diet was assessed with food frequency questionnaires. Over an average follow-up of 12 years, the scans showed the expected age-related changes, including decreases in total brain, grey matter and hippocampal volumes, and increases in the fluid-filled ventricles.

However, people with higher MIND diet scores had slower loss of grey matter, which plays an important role in memory, learning, decision making and information processing. The average score was just under 7 out of a possible 15. Each 3 point increase in score was associated with 20% less age-related decline, which the researchers said was equivalent to 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. A similar pattern appeared in ventricle enlargement, where each 3 point rise was associated with 8% less tissue loss and about 1 year of delayed brain aging.

Some foods seemed to matter more. Higher berry intake was linked to slower ventricle growth, and poultry was linked to slower ventricle growth and a slower decline in grey matter. Higher consumption of sweets was associated with faster ventricle enlargement and greater hippocampal atrophy, and fried fast foods were linked to a larger decline in hippocampal volume.

The findings describe associations. People with the highest diet scores were also more likely to be women and college educated and less likely to smoke or have obesity, so diet may not be the only factor involved.
why_it_matters: The study suggests that long-term eating habits may be connected to how the brain changes with age, but because it shows associations, more research is needed before anyone can say food is the cause.

No changes at all in any participant

options: Skipping every meal
Eating more fried fast foods
Higher MIND diet scores
Lower MIND diet scores

questions.question: According to the researchers, what did each 3 point increase in score correspond to for grey matter?
options: 15% more age-related decline, or 2.5 years of aging
20% less age-related decline, or 2.5 years of delayed aging
8% less tissue loss, or about 1 year of delayed aging
No difference compared with lower scores
questions.correct_answer: 20% less age-related decline, or 2.5 years of delayed aging

questions.question: Which foods were linked to faster ventricle enlargement or hippocampal decline?
options: Olive oil and whole grains
Sweets and fried fast foods

questions.question: Why does the story say diet may not be the only factor?
options: The study only included people who had a stroke
The scores were collected on a single day
All participants ate exactly the same foods
People with high scores also differed in other ways, such as smoking and education
questions.correct_answer: People with high scores also differed in other ways, such as smoking and education

background_read: An observational study watches what happens to people over time instead of assigning them to different diets, so it can show links but cannot easily prove cause and effect.
Neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, are conditions in which brain cells are gradually damaged.
